title: What Makes a Car Worth Its Price?
section: Horsepower vs. MSRP by Vehicle Body Style
text:
Horsepower vs. MSRP by Vehicle Body Style



Code
# Prepare hover text for interactive exploration
plot_df <- msrp_df |>
  mutate(
    hover_label = paste0(
      "<b>", year, " ", make, " ", model, "</b><br>",
      "Body Style: ", body_style, " (", body_group, ")<br>",
      "Horsepower: ", comma(horsepower), " hp<br>",
      "MSRP: ", dollar(msrp), "<br>",
      "Fuel Economy: ", mpg_city, " city / ", mpg_highway, " hwy MPG"
    )
  )

p_home <- ggplot(
  plot_df,
  aes(
    x = horsepower,
    y = msrp,
    color = body_group,
    text = hover_label
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.7) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = label_dollar(),
    breaks = c(10000, 25000, 50000, 100000, 250000, 500000, 1500000)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "Coupe" = "#d90429",
    "Convertible" = "#ef233c",
    "Sedan" = "#9e1b32",
    "Hatchback" = "#ff5964",
    "Wagon" = "#6d6d6d",
    "SUV" = "#111111",
    "Van / Minivan" = "#4a4a4a",
    "Pickup" = "#262626"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Vehicle Sticker Price Rises Steeply With Horsepower (N = ", comma(n_msrp), " Vehicles)"),
    x = "Engine Horsepower (HP)",
    y = "Manufacturer Suggested Retail Price (MSRP, log scale)",
    color = "Body Style"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

ggplotly(p_home, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.18),
    margin = list(b = 90)
  )








Figure 1






Key Takeaways & Data Filtering Notes

Exponential price scaling: Doubling horsepower from 150 HP to 300 HP moves typical vehicles from economy hatchbacks and compact sedans (~$18,000–$24,000) into mid-tier SUVs, pickups, and sport sedans (~$35,000–$50,000), while Coupes and Convertibles above 500 HP surge past $100,000.
Transparent filtering (11,914 \(\rightarrow\) 9,762 rows): Starting from the 11,914 raw rows in cars_msrp_kaggle.csv, we removed 715 exact duplicate rows, excluded 1,368 pre-2001 observations (which recorded $2,000 used trade-in estimates rather than original new-car MSRPs), and dropped 69 rows missing engine horsepower—leaving 9,762 verified new-vehicle observations.
Connecting recent vehicles (2022–2027): Because Trimslate’s public CSV export omits MSRP values, all price graphics use verified msrp_merged.csv observations while our Car Explorer, Fuel Economy, and Automotive Trends tabs focus on 7,397 recent 2022–2027 vehicles and 1975–2025 EPA records.

title: What Makes a Car Worth Its Price?
text:
Research Question
How do vehicle price, horsepower, fuel economy, and manufacturer relate to one another in recent vehicles?
Combining manufacturer suggested retail prices (MSRP), Trimslate vehicle specifications (through model year 2027), and U.S. EPA certification and historical trend records (1975–2025), this website investigates what buyers gain in performance and efficiency as vehicle prices climb.

title: Price & Performance
text:
Code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(scales)

msrp_df <- read_csv("data/processed/msrp_merged.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
recent_df <- read_csv("data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

n_total_msrp <- nrow(msrp_df)
n_mainstream <- sum(msrp_df$msrp <= 250000)
n_exotic_outliers <- sum(msrp_df$msrp > 250000)
n_recent_hp <- sum(!is.na(recent_df$horsepower_combined))

title: Price & Performance
text:
Overview & Available Performance Variables
To test whether higher vehicle prices buy proportionally more engine performance—or whether buyers primarily pay for body style and brand prestige—we examine 9,762 deduplicated new-vehicle observations from msrp_merged.csv alongside 7,397 recent 2022–2027 trims from recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv.

Available variables used here: horsepower (engine HP), msrp (sticker price in USD), make (manufacturer), model, year, and body_group (8 consolidated vehicle body styles).
Why torque is omitted: Inspection of all cleaned datasets confirmed that torque is 100% missing (0 non-NA values out of 7,397 rows) in Trimslate’s public CSV export and is not recorded in either the MSRP dataset or EPA certification tables. Rather than imputing or fabricating values, we focus strictly on verified horsepower and MSRP records.

title: Price & Performance
section: 1. Horsepower vs. MSRP Grouped by Vehicle Body Style
text:
1. Horsepower vs. MSRP Grouped by Vehicle Body Style
To compare the linear dollar-per-horsepower relationship across body styles without million-dollar hypercars compressing the vertical axis, the faceted chart below displays 9,602 vehicles priced at or below $250,000 (98.4% of our 9,762 MSRP observations, excluding 160 ultra-exotic outliers up to $2,065,902).



Code
# Filter extreme >$250k supercar outliers so linear slopes within each body style are legible
faceted_df <- msrp_df |>
  filter(msrp <= 250000) |>
  mutate(
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, " ", make, " ", model, "</b><br>",
      "Body Style: ", body_style, "<br>",
      "Horsepower: ", comma(horsepower), " hp<br>",
      "MSRP: ", dollar(msrp)
    )
  )

p_body_scatter <- ggplot(
  faceted_df,
  aes(x = horsepower, y = msrp, color = body_group)
) +
  geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), alpha = 0.4, size = 1.3) +
  # Linear trend line per body style (inherit.aes = FALSE avoids hover text warnings)
  geom_smooth(
    aes(x = horsepower, y = msrp),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#1b2838",
    linewidth = 0.7,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ body_group, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Horsepower vs. MSRP Within Each Body Style (N = ",
      comma(n_mainstream), " Vehicles <= $250k)"
    ),
    x = "Engine Horsepower (hp)",
    y = "MSRP ($ Thousands)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggplotly(p_body_scatter, tooltip = "text")








Figure 1





Patterns & Findings: Every body style exhibits a positive relationship between horsepower and MSRP, but the price slope varies dramatically by segment. Coupes and Convertibles climb steepest past 300 hp—frequently crossing $100,000–$250,000—whereas Pickups and Vans / Minivans cluster tightly between $20,000 and $55,000 even when equipped with 300–400 hp V6 and V8 towing engines. Hatchbacks occupy the most compact, budget-focused corner (100–250 hp, mostly under $30,000).

title: Price & Performance
text:
2. Horsepower per Dollar Across Manufacturers
Which brands deliver the most raw engine output for your money, and which charge a luxury premium? Below, we calculate horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP (alongside exact HP per $1 in the hover tooltip) across all 38 manufacturers with at least 30 vehicles in our dataset (N = 9,681 vehicles; 81 vehicles from 9 tiny boutique brands with <30 models are excluded so small samples do not skew brand averages).



Code
mfr_summary <- msrp_df |>
  mutate(
    hp_per_1k = horsepower / (msrp / 1000),
    hp_per_dollar = horsepower / msrp
  ) |>
  summarize(
    n_models = n(),
    mean_hp_per_1k = mean(hp_per_1k),
    mean_hp_per_dollar = mean(hp_per_dollar),
    mean_hp = mean(horsepower),
    mean_msrp = mean(msrp),
    .by = make
  ) |>
  filter(n_models >= 30) |>
  mutate(
    make = fct_reorder(make, mean_hp_per_1k),
    tier = case_when(
      mean_msrp >= 100000 ~ "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury (Mean MSRP >= $100k)",
      mean_msrp >= 40000 ~ "Luxury / Near-Luxury ($40k-$99k)",
      TRUE ~ "Mainstream (< $40k)"
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", make, "</b> (n = ", comma(n_models), " vehicles)<br>",
      "Avg Value: ", round(mean_hp_per_1k, 2), " hp per $1,000 (",
      round(mean_hp_per_dollar, 4), " hp/$)<br>",
      "Avg Horsepower: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp<br>",
      "Avg MSRP: ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0))
    )
  )

n_mfr_vehicles <- sum(mfr_summary$n_models)

p_mfr <- ggplot(
  mfr_summary,
  aes(x = mean_hp_per_1k, y = make, fill = tier, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " hp/$1k")) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Mainstream (< $40k)" = "#2b8cbe",
      "Luxury / Near-Luxury ($40k-$99k)" = "#7bccc4",
      "Exotic / Ultra-Luxury (Mean MSRP >= $100k)" = "#084081"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Average Horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP Across 38 Manufacturers (N = ",
      comma(n_mfr_vehicles), " Vehicles)"
    ),
    x = "Average Horsepower per $1,000 of MSRP",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Market Segment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_mfr, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.1),
    margin = list(b = 80)
  )








Figure 2





Patterns & Findings: Mainstream brands dominate raw horsepower-per-dollar value: Dodge leads all manufacturers at 9.16 hp per $1,000 (0.0092 hp/$, averaging 280 hp at $31,182), followed by Suzuki (8.47), Pontiac (8.45), Kia (8.37), Chevrolet (8.12), and Hyundai (8.11). Conversely, luxury and exotic badges sit at the bottom—BMW (5.44), Mercedes-Benz (5.08), Porsche (4.01), Ferrari (2.23), and Rolls-Royce (1.48 hp per $1,000)—demonstrating diminishing horsepower returns per dollar as buyers pay for craftsmanship, chassis engineering, and brand exclusivity.

title: Price & Performance
section: 3. Average MSRP Across Vehicle Body Styles
text:
3. Average MSRP Across Vehicle Body Styles
Finally, we compare average MSRP across all eight consolidated body styles using the full N = 9,762 dataset (including exotic models, while reporting median MSRP and the <= $250k trimmed average in each bar’s tooltip to show the effect of high-end outliers).



Code
body_summary <- msrp_df |>
  summarize(
    n_vehicles = n(),
    mean_msrp = mean(msrp),
    median_msrp = median(msrp),
    trimmed_mean_msrp = mean(msrp[msrp <= 250000]),
    mean_hp = mean(horsepower),
    .by = body_group
  ) |>
  mutate(
    body_group = fct_reorder(body_group, mean_msrp),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", body_group, "</b> (n = ", comma(n_vehicles), " vehicles)<br>",
      "Average MSRP (all): ", dollar(round(mean_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Median MSRP: ", dollar(round(median_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Average MSRP (<= $250k): ", dollar(round(trimmed_mean_msrp, 0)), "<br>",
      "Average Horsepower: ", round(mean_hp, 0), " hp"
    )
  )

p_body_msrp <- ggplot(
  body_summary,
  aes(x = mean_msrp, y = body_group, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c3e50", width = 0.68) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Average MSRP by Vehicle Body Style (N = ",
      comma(n_total_msrp), " Vehicles)"
    ),
    x = "Average MSRP (USD)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_body_msrp, tooltip = "text")








Figure 3





Patterns & Findings: Convertibles ($96,084 mean; $49,850 median) and Coupes ($92,495 mean; $46,150 median) carry more than double the average MSRP of any other body style—partly because almost all six- and seven-figure supercars take two-door coupe or roadster form (even excluding >$250k exotics, Convertibles average $72,145 and Coupes $68,079). Mainstream utility and family styles sit much closer to their medians: Sedans ($45,424 mean / $32,970 median), SUVs ($41,313 mean / $35,800 median), Pickups ($32,724), Vans / Minivans ($30,603), Wagons ($30,120), and entry-level Hatchbacks ($23,364).

title: Price & Performance
section: Limitations: Comparing 2001–2017 MSRP Data With 2022–2027 Vehicles
text:
Limitations: Comparing 2001–2017 MSRP Data With 2022–2027 Vehicles
Because our price analysis relies on msrp_merged.csv (2001–2017) while our recent specification tabs use recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv (2022–2027), three concrete limitations apply:

Post-2017 price inflation is not captured in nominal MSRPs: U.S. new-vehicle transaction and sticker prices rose substantially after 2020, so a $33,050 median MSRP in our 2001–2017 data reflects earlier nominal dollars rather than 2022–2027 showroom stickers.
Higher baseline horsepower in 2022–2027: Across the 2,669 recent 2022–2027 trims with certified engine output, horsepower averages 330.2 hp (median 305 hp), up from 265 hp (median 252 hp) in our 2001–2017 MSRP dataset due to widespread turbocharging and larger SUV/truck lineups.
Electrified powertrain gaps: Modern battery-electric vehicles (EVs) and full hybrids—which play a major role in 2022–2027 pricing and acceleration—had minimal market share prior to 2017 and frequently lack combined system horsepower in EPA engine-certification tables. For those vehicles, we avoid merging incompatible years and instead examine recent powertrains directly on the Fuel Economy and Car Explorer pages.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
text:
Code
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(scales)

recent_df <- read_csv("data/processed/recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

n_recent_total <- nrow(recent_df)
mpg_df <- recent_df |> filter(!is.na(mpg_city), !is.na(mpg_highway), !is.na(powertrain))
n_mpg <- nrow(mpg_df)

ev_df <- recent_df |>
  filter(powertrain == "Electric", !is.na(electric_range), electric_range > 0)
n_ev_total <- nrow(ev_df)

cost_df <- recent_df |> filter(!is.na(annual_fuel_cost), !is.na(powertrain))
n_cost <- nrow(cost_df)

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
text:
Overview & Unit Definitions (2022–2027 Vehicles)
Using 7,397 recent vehicle trims (model years 2022–2027) from recent_vehicles_2022_2027.csv, 7,149 trims carry complete EPA city and highway efficiency ratings (248 unrated heavy-duty or pre-release trims are excluded from MPG charts rather than imputed).

MPG vs. MPGe: For Gas, Hybrid, and Diesel vehicles, EPA reports miles per gallon of liquid fuel (MPG). For Electric vehicles (EVs), EPA reports miles per gallon equivalent (MPGe, where 33.7 kWh of electricity equals the energy content of one gallon of gasoline).
EV Range vs. PHEV Tank Range: Inspection of the raw Trimslate data showed that Plug-in Hybrid rows (n = 232) record total combined gas + battery range (~360–430+ miles) in electric_range, whereas Electric rows (N = 1,428 pure battery-electric trims) record true single-charge battery range. Accordingly, our EV range comparison includes verified battery-electric vehicles only.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
section: 1. City vs. Highway Efficiency Across Powertrains
text:
1. City vs. Highway Efficiency Across Powertrains
How do stop-and-go city driving and steady highway cruising affect different powertrains? The dashed diagonal line below marks equal city and highway efficiency (Highway = City) across N = 7,149 rated 2022–2027 trims.



Code
mpg_plot_df <- mpg_df |>
  mutate(
    unit_label = if_else(powertrain == "Electric", "MPGe", "MPG"),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, " ", make, " ", model, "</b><br>",
      "Trim: ", trim, "<br>",
      "Powertrain: ", powertrain, " (", body_group, ")<br>",
      "City: ", mpg_city, " ", unit_label,
      " | Highway: ", mpg_highway, " ", unit_label, "<br>",
      "Combined: ", mpg_combined, " ", unit_label
    )
  )

p_city_hwy <- ggplot(
  mpg_plot_df,
  aes(x = mpg_city, y = mpg_highway, color = powertrain, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#4a5568",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.7) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "City vs. Highway Efficiency by Powertrain (N = ",
      comma(n_mpg), " Trims, MY 2022-2027)"
    ),
    x = "City Efficiency (MPG for Fuel / MPGe for Electric)",
    y = "Highway Efficiency (MPG for Fuel / MPGe for Electric)",
    color = "Powertrain"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_city_hwy, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.16),
    margin = list(b = 85)
  )








Figure 1





Patterns & Findings: Notice how Gas (n = 4,233) and Diesel (n = 126) trims sit consistently above the dashed parity line, averaging 26.1 highway MPG vs. 19.7 city MPG because combustion engines waste energy idling and braking in traffic. Hybrids (n = 1,130) close that gap (26.9 city / 30.8 highway MPG), while Electric vehicles (n = 1,428) flip below the parity line—averaging 97.3 city MPGe vs. 87.1 highway MPGe—because regenerative braking recaptures city deceleration energy while aerodynamic drag rises at highway speeds.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
text:
2. Battery-Electric Driving Range Across Manufacturers
Among pure battery-electric vehicles (powertrain == "Electric"), single-charge EPA range averages 297.1 miles across all 1,428 trims (2022–2027). Below, we compare the 26 manufacturers with at least 10 rated EV trims, coloring bars by average combined MPGe to distinguish aerodynamic efficiency from sheer battery size.



Code
ev_mfr <- ev_df |>
  summarize(
    n_trims = n(),
    mean_range = mean(electric_range),
    max_range = max(electric_range),
    mean_mpge = mean(mpg_combined, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_cost = mean(annual_fuel_cost, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = make
  ) |>
  filter(n_trims >= 10) |>
  mutate(
    make = fct_reorder(make, mean_range),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", make, "</b> (n = ", n_trims, " EV trims)<br>",
      "Average EV Range: ", round(mean_range, 1), " miles<br>",
      "Longest-Range Trim: ", round(max_range, 0), " miles<br>",
      "Average Combined Efficiency: ", round(mean_mpge, 1), " MPGe<br>",
      "Avg Annual Electricity Cost: ", dollar(round(mean_cost, 0))
    )
  )

n_ev_mfr_trims <- sum(ev_mfr$n_trims)

p_ev_range <- ggplot(
  ev_mfr,
  aes(x = mean_range, y = make, fill = mean_mpge, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " mi")) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", direction = -1) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Average EPA Single-Charge Range Across 26 EV Makers (N = ",
      comma(n_ev_mfr_trims), " EV Trims)"
    ),
    x = "Average EPA Electric Driving Range (Miles)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Avg MPGe"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_ev_range, tooltip = "text")








Figure 2





Patterns & Findings: Lucid leads the industry by nearly 90 miles (425.7 miles average; 520 miles peak on the Air Dream Edition) while maintaining top-tier efficiency (116.0 MPGe). By contrast, comparing bar length with color exposes two very different engineering paths past 320 miles: Tesla (328.4 mi, 114.0 MPGe) achieves long range through lightweight aerodynamics, whereas electric pickup makers Chevrolet (336.1 mi, 86.7 MPGe), Rivian (331.4 mi, 76.3 MPGe), and GMC (322.2 mi, 55.5 MPGe) rely on massive battery packs that consume roughly twice as much electricity per mile.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
section: 3. EPA Estimated Annual Fuel & Electricity Cost by Powertrain
text:
3. EPA Estimated Annual Fuel & Electricity Cost by Powertrain
How much do efficiency differences save drivers each year? Using EPA’s standardized annual energy cost estimates across N = 7,126 trims (2022–2027), we compare average annual running costs by powertrain.



Code
cost_summary <- cost_df |>
  summarize(
    n_trims = n(),
    mean_cost = mean(annual_fuel_cost),
    median_cost = median(annual_fuel_cost),
    mean_comb = mean(mpg_combined, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = powertrain
  ) |>
  mutate(
    powertrain = fct_reorder(powertrain, mean_cost),
    unit_label = if_else(powertrain == "Electric", "MPGe", "MPG"),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", powertrain, "</b> (n = ", comma(n_trims), " trims)<br>",
      "Average Annual Cost: ", dollar(round(mean_cost, 0)), "/yr<br>",
      "Median Annual Cost: ", dollar(round(median_cost, 0)), "/yr<br>",
      "Avg Combined Rating: ", round(mean_comb, 1), " ", unit_label
    )
  )

p_cost <- ggplot(
  cost_summary,
  aes(x = mean_cost, y = powertrain, fill = powertrain, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar(suffix = "/yr")) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Average EPA Annual Fuel / Electricity Cost by Powertrain (N = ",
      comma(n_cost), " Trims, MY 2022-2027)"
    ),
    x = "Estimated Annual Fuel / Energy Cost (USD / Year)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggplotly(p_cost, tooltip = "text")








Figure 3





Patterns & Findings: Electric vehicles average just $847/year in estimated electricity costs ($850 median)—saving roughly $2,510 per year ($12,550 over five years) compared with conventional Gas vehicles ($3,357/year) and $2,880/year compared with truck-heavy Diesel trims ($3,727/year). Conventional Hybrids ($2,879/year) trim about $478/year off average gasoline fuel bills without requiring home charging infrastructure.

Full Interactive Search & Filter Table (N = 7,397 trims): Filter all 2022–2027 trims by manufacturer, model, year, body style, powertrain, horsepower, MPG/MPGe, electric range, and annual fuel cost.

title: Car Explorer
text:
1. Featured Vehicle Gallery & Attribution


Code
# Match each downloaded image to the newest well-populated 2024-2027 trim for that make & model
featured_specs <- img_df |>
  pmap(\(make, model_prefix, local_image, commons_file, source_url, photographer, license, license_url) {
    matches <- recent_df |>
      filter(
        .data$make == .env$make,
        str_detect(model, fixed(model_prefix, ignore_case = TRUE)),
        !is.na(mpg_combined)
      ) |>
      # Prefer trims that also have certified horsepower when available
      arrange(is.na(horsepower_combined), desc(year))

    top_row <- slice_head(matches, n = 1)
    bind_cols(
      top_row,
      tibble(
        local_image = local_image,
        source_url = source_url,
        photographer = photographer,
        license = license,
        license_url = license_url
      )
    )
  }) |>
  list_rbind()

render_vehicle_cards <- function(df) {
  cards <- pmap(df, function(...) {
    row <- list(...)
    eff_unit <- if (identical(row$powertrain, "Electric")) "MPGe" else "MPG"
    hp_label <- if (!is.na(row$horsepower_combined)) {
      paste0(comma(row$horsepower_combined), " hp")
    } else {
      "Not rated (EV/Hybrid)"
    }
    range_line <- if (identical(row$powertrain, "Electric") && !is.na(row$electric_range) && row$electric_range > 0) {
      tags$div(tags$strong("EV Range: "), paste0(row$electric_range, " miles"))
    } else {
      NULL
    }
    cost_label <- if (!is.na(row$annual_fuel_cost)) dollar(row$annual_fuel_cost) else "N/A"

    div(
      style = "background:#ffffff; border:1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius:0.6rem; overflow:hidden; display:flex; flex-direction:column; justify-content:space-between;",
      div(
        tags$img(
          src = row$local_image,
          alt = paste(row$year, row$make, row$model),
          style = "width:100%; height:185px; object-fit:cover; border-bottom:1px solid #e2e8f0;"
        ),
        div(
          style = "padding:0.9rem 1rem;",
          tags$h4(
            style = "margin:0 0 0.25rem 0; font-size:1.05rem;",
            paste(row$year, row$make, row$model)
          ),
          tags$div(
            style = "font-size:0.82rem; color:#4a5568; margin-bottom:0.55rem;",
            paste0(row$powertrain, " · ", row$body_group)
          ),
          tags$div(
            style = "font-size:0.88rem; line-height:1.5;",
            tags$div(tags$strong("Horsepower: "), hp_label),
            tags$div(
              tags$strong("Efficiency: "),
              paste0(row$mpg_city, " city / ", row$mpg_highway, " hwy ", eff_unit)
            ),
            range_line,
            tags$div(tags$strong("Est. Fuel/Energy Cost: "), paste0(cost_label, "/yr"))
          )
        )
      ),
      div(
        style = "background:#f8f9fa; border-top:1px solid #edf2f7; padding:0.5rem 1rem; font-size:0.74rem; color:#4a5568;",
        "Photo: ", row$photographer, " · ",
        tags$a(href = row$license_url, target = "_blank", rel = "noopener", row$license),
        " · ",
        tags$a(href = row$source_url, target = "_blank", rel = "noopener", "Source")
      )
    )
  })

  div(
    style = "display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill, minmax(270px, 1fr)); gap:1.1rem; margin:1rem 0;",
    cards
  )
}

title: Car Explorer
text:
2. Search & Filter All 2022–2027 Vehicles (N = 7,397 Trims)
Use the Search box at top right or the column filter boxes directly beneath each column header to filter by model year, manufacturer, model, body style, powertrain, horsepower, efficiency, EV range, or annual fuel cost.


Code
explorer_table <- recent_df |>
  mutate(
    ev_range_only = if_else(powertrain == "Electric", electric_range, NA_real_)
  ) |>
  select(
    Year = year,
    Make = make,
    Model = model,
    Trim = trim,
    `Body Style` = body_group,
    Powertrain = powertrain,
    `HP` = horsepower_combined,
    `City` = mpg_city,
    `Hwy` = mpg_highway,
    `EV Range (mi)` = ev_range_only,
    `Fuel Cost ($/yr)` = annual_fuel_cost
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Make = as.factor(Make),
    `Body Style` = as.factor(`Body Style`),
    Powertrain = as.factor(Powertrain)
  )

datatable(
  explorer_table,
  filter = "top",
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 15,
    scrollX = TRUE,
    autoWidth = TRUE
  ),
  caption = htmltools::tags$caption(
    style = "caption-side: top; text-align: left; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;",
    paste0(
      "Interactive 2022-2027 Vehicle Specifications Explorer (N = ",
      comma(n_recent),
      " Trims; City/Hwy reported in MPG for fuel vehicles and MPGe for Electric vehicles)"
    )
  )
) |>
  formatCurrency("Fuel Cost ($/yr)", currency = "$", digits = 0) |>
  formatRound(c("HP", "City", "Hwy", "EV Range (mi)"), digits = 0)
